title: Entropy and information
bigIdea: Information measures how much uncertainty an outcome removes, while entropy is the average surprise of a source; the same ideas explain compression, dependence, model mismatch, and reliable communication.

concepts.title: Coin flips as a playground for uncertainty
concepts.summary: A coin flip has outcomes with probabilities, and a fair flip leaves two equally plausible possibilities before it lands. Repeating flips gives us a concrete source whose uncertainty we can count.
concepts.intuition: A flip is a tiny question asked by nature: before the answer arrives, the possible answers share a limited amount of uncertainty.
misconceptions: A random outcome has no structure or probability at all.
A fair coin must alternate heads and tails over a short run.
A run that looks unusual makes the next independent flip compensate for it.
visualHooks: A two-door fork that closes to one door when the coin lands.
A growing tray of flips whose heads and tails settle toward their probabilities.
A curious blob choosing between two equally bright planets.

concepts.title: Probability assigns weight to possibilities
concepts.summary: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 that describes how often an outcome is expected in repeated trials or how strongly a model weights that outcome. All mutually exclusive outcomes together have total probability 1.
concepts.intuition: Probability is the share of a possibility pie that an outcome owns before the experiment reveals it.
misconceptions: A probability of 0.7 guarantees exactly 70 successes in the next 100 trials.
Probability is only a subjective feeling and cannot describe repeatable frequencies.
If one outcome becomes less likely, every other named outcome must become equally likely.
visualHooks: Slices of a unit circle becoming a weighted coin.
A stream of trials with a running frequency line approaching a target.
Buckets of probability mass that always add to one.

concepts.title: Surprise is minus log probability
concepts.summary: The information or surprise of an outcome with probability p is I(x) = -log₂ p(x). Certain outcomes carry 0 bits, while rarer outcomes carry more bits because they eliminate more plausible alternatives.
concepts.intuition: Surprise is the number of fair yes-or-no questions needed to single out an outcome that had probability p.
misconceptions: A rare outcome is intrinsically more important than a common outcome.
Surprise should be proportional to p, so a likely outcome should feel more informative.
The logarithm is an arbitrary decoration rather than the rule that makes independent surprises add.
visualHooks: A rare door requiring a tall stack of binary questions to locate.
A probability slider whose surprise meter rises as its outcome becomes rare.
Two independent question trees joining end-to-end to show log addition.

concepts.title: Expected surprise averages outcomes
concepts.summary: A source's expected surprise is the probability-weighted average of its outcome surprises: E[I(X)] = Σ p(x)(-log₂ p(x)). Common outcomes count often and rare outcomes count a lot per occurrence.
concepts.intuition: Expected surprise asks what the long-run information per message will be when the source keeps speaking.
misconceptions: The most surprising possible outcome is the source's average information.
A rare event can be ignored because it hardly ever appears.
Averages should weight each named outcome equally even when their probabilities differ.
visualHooks: A balance scale with each outcome's probability as its weight and surprise as its height.
A long stream of messages whose cumulative bits settle to an average slope.
A roulette of outcomes feeding a running weighted sum.

concepts.title: Entropy is average uncertainty
concepts.summary: Entropy H(X) = -Σ p(x) log₂ p(x) is the expected surprise of a random variable. It is largest when the possible outcomes are equally likely and smaller when probability is concentrated.
concepts.intuition: Entropy is the source's uncertainty budget per symbol, measured by how many binary decisions its messages require on average.
misconceptions: Entropy is the surprise of one particular outcome.
A source with more named outcomes must always have more entropy.
Entropy measures disorder in a physical object rather than uncertainty in a probability distribution.
visualHooks: A probability landscape flattening to its highest uncertainty at uniformity.
A pile of binary questions whose average height is labeled H(X).
Two coins, one fair and one heavily biased, compared by their uncertainty clouds.

concepts.title: Bits count binary alternatives
concepts.summary: A bit is one binary digit and also the information in one fair binary choice. Entropy measured with log₂ is measured in bits, so a fair coin has entropy 1 bit per flip.
concepts.intuition: One bit is one clean fork with two equally plausible branches; many bits are a path through many such forks.
misconceptions: A bit always means a physical transistor or a single stored 0/1 value.
A biased coin still has exactly one bit of entropy because it has two labels.
Bits and bytes are interchangeable units.
visualHooks: A binary question tree with one level labeled one bit.
A tape of fair-flip answers turning into a stream of 0s and 1s.
A measuring ruler marked in binary forks rather than centimeters.

concepts.title: Cross-entropy scores a predictive model
concepts.summary: Cross-entropy H(P,Q) = Eₚ[-log₂ Q(x)] is the average code length or surprise assigned by model Q when reality follows P. It rewards assigning high probability to what actually occurs.
concepts.intuition: Cross-entropy is the bill for using someone else's probability forecast to describe messages generated by the real source.
misconceptions: Cross-entropy compares only the names of outcomes and ignores their probabilities.
A model can assign zero probability to an event and receive a finite penalty when that event occurs.
Cross-entropy is always symmetric between P and Q.
visualHooks: A messenger using a mismatched question tree and paying extra binary questions.
Two probability bars, P and Q, with Q's predictions tested by P's outcomes.
A scoreboard of average bits per symbol under different forecasts.

concepts.title: Joint entropy counts pairs together
concepts.summary: Joint entropy H(X,Y) is the entropy of the pair, H(X,Y) = -Σ p(x,y) log₂ p(x,y). It counts the average information needed to identify both variables together.
concepts.intuition: A pair is one larger outcome space: joint entropy measures how many binary questions identify the row-and-column answer together.
misconceptions: Joint entropy is always the sum of the two individual entropies.
Knowing one variable can never change how much information the pair needs.
The order of the variables changes the value of H(X,Y).
visualHooks: A grid of paired outcomes with probability mass painted into each cell.
Two answer cards stapled together and counted as one combined symbol.
A branching tree that first asks X and then asks Y.

concepts.title: Conditional entropy is uncertainty left over
concepts.summary: Conditional entropy H(Y|X) is the average uncertainty in Y after X is known. The chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X) separates the questions needed for X from those still needed for Y.
concepts.intuition: Conditional entropy is the part of a question that remains after a clue has already crossed out some possibilities.
misconceptions: Conditioning on any extra variable must increase uncertainty.
H(Y|X) and H(X|Y) are generally the same number.
If X and Y are correlated, conditional entropy must be zero.
visualHooks: A foggy possibility cloud shrinking after a clue reveals X.
A two-stage question tree with the remaining depth highlighted.
Several conditional distributions, one for each observed X, averaged together.

concepts.title: Mutual information measures shared knowledge
concepts.summary: Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) measures how many bits knowing one variable tells us about the other. It is zero for independent variables.
concepts.intuition: Mutual information is the overlap between two uncertainty clouds: the bits one observation reliably predicts about the other.
misconceptions: Mutual information is a directional amount like H(Y|X) and must differ when X and Y swap.
A high correlation coefficient is the only way variables can share information.
Zero mutual information means the variables have no relationship of any kind in every setting.
visualHooks: Two translucent entropy circles whose overlap is labeled shared bits.
A clue about X erasing a measured amount of uncertainty about Y.
A scatter of paired outcomes collapsing from a rectangle to a diagonal when dependence grows.

concepts.title: KL divergence is the cost of a wrong model
concepts.summary: Kullback–Leibler divergence Dₖₗ(P‖Q) = Σ p(x) log₂(p(x)/q(x)) equals H(P,Q) - H(P): the extra average bits paid when coding P-generated data with model Q. It is nonnegative and generally asymmetric.
concepts.intuition: KL divergence is the wasted coding room caused by believing the source follows Q when it actually follows P.
misconceptions: KL divergence is a true distance and must be symmetric.
A negative KL divergence is a normal result when Q predicts a frequent outcome too strongly.
The divergence is zero whenever P and Q have the same set of possible labels, even if weights differ.
visualHooks: An ideal question tree beside a mismatched tree, with the extra branches highlighted.
P probability mass walking through Q's forecast and leaving a trail of wasted bits.
An asymmetric arrow between distributions, showing that direction matters.

concepts.title: Redundancy can defeat a noisy channel
concepts.summary: A communication channel can flip or erase symbols, but carefully designed redundancy lets a receiver infer the intended message. Shannon's channel capacity is the maximum reliable information rate, expressed through mutual information.
concepts.intuition: A noisy channel is a blurry pipe: send slowly enough and add the right structure, and the receiver can recover the message despite individual errors.
misconceptions: Repeating every bit many times always reaches perfect reliability at no cost.
More noise can always be overcome by sending more symbols per second.
Compression and error correction are the same operation with different names.
visualHooks: A message of colored beads crossing a shaking tube, then being restored by a patterned code.
A noisy scatter plot of received symbols with decision regions around codewords.
A capacity speed limit sign separating reliable from unreliable communication rates.
